etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English spede (“prosperity, good luck, quickness, success”), from Old English spēd (“success”), from Proto-West Germanic *spōdi (“prosperity, success”), from Proto-West Germanic *spōan, from Proto-Germanic *spōaną (“to prosper, succeed, be happy”), from Proto-Indo-European *speh₁- (“to prosper, turn out well”). Cognate with Scots spede, speid (“success, quickness, speed”), Dutch spoed (“haste; speed”), German Low German Spood (“haste; speed; eagerness; success”), German Sput (“progress, acceleration, haste”). Related also to Old English spōwan (“to be successful, succeed”), Albanian shpejt (“to speed, to hurry”) and Russian спеши́ть (spešítʹ, “to hurry”), Latin spēs (“hope, expectation”), spērō (“hope”, verb), perhaps also to Ancient Greek σπεύδω (speúdō, “to urge on, hasten, press on”).

definitions.definition: The state of moving quickly or the capacity for rapid motion.

quote.citation: c. 1587–1588, [Christopher Marlowe], Tamburlaine the Great.  […]  The First Part […], 2nd edition, part 1, London:  […]  [R. Robinson for] Richard Iones, […], published 1592, →OCLC; reprinted as Tamburlaine the Great (A Scolar Press Facsimile), Menston, Yorkshire, London: Scolar Press, 1973, →ISBN, Act I, scene i:
quote.text: Returne with ſpeed, time paſſeth ſwift away,Our life is fraile, and we may dye to day.

definitions.definition: (mathematics, physics) The rate of motion or action, specifically  the magnitude of the velocity; the rate distance is traversed in a given time.

quote.citation: 1960 December, “Talking of Trains: Recording Electric Operation”, in Trains Illustrated, London: Ian Allan Publishing, →ISSN, →OCLC, page 707:
quote.text: Train positions and speeds were established by a track magnet at each milepost, which produced a suitable mark on the punched recording tape whenever a train passed.

definitions.definition: (photography) The sensitivity to light of film, plates or sensor.
(photography) The duration of exposure, the time during which a camera shutter is open (shutter speed).
(photography) The largest size of the lens opening at which a lens can be used.
(photography) The ratio of the focal length to the diameter of a photographic objective.
(slang, uncountable) Amphetamine or any amphetamine-based drug (especially methamphetamine) used as a stimulant, especially illegally.
(archaic) Luck, success, prosperity.

quote.citation: c. 1591–1595 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Romeo and Ivliet”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene iii], page 76:
quote.text: St. Francis be my ſpeed, how oft to night / Haue my old feet ſtumbled at graues?

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Genesis 24:12:
quote.text: O Lord God of my master Abraham, I pray thee, send me good speed this day.

definitions.definition: (slang) Personal preference.

quote.citation: 2024 April 8, Nikki Ogunnaike, “3 Outfit Formulas That Will Carry You Through Any Season”, in Marie Claire‎[1]:
quote.text: I used to dream of throwing on the heritage Burberry coat and teaming it with Hunter wellies (which is admittedly a very cute look), but a few years ago I realized an oversize option is actually my speed.

definitions.definition: (finance, uncountable) A third-order measure of derivative price sensitivity, expressed as the rate of change of gamma with respect to changes in the underlying asset price.
(film) Called by the soundman when the recording equipment has reached running speed and is ready to go.

quote.citation: 2012, Tom Mascaro, Into the Fray, page 52:
quote.text: […]  the director called, “Roll 'em,” the sound man said, “Speed,” and Norling stepped in and said,  […]

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English speden, from Old English spēdan (“to speed, prosper, succeed, have success”), from Proto-West Germanic *spōdijan (“to succeed”). Cognate with Scots spede, speid (“to meet with success, assist, promote, accomplish, speed”), Dutch spoeden (“to hurry, rush”), Low German spoden, spöden (“to hasten, speed”), German sputen, spuden (“to speed”).

definitions.definition: (intransitive, archaic) To succeed; to prosper, be lucky.

quote.citation: 1485, Sir Thomas Malory, chapter 1, in Le Morte Darthur, book I:
quote.text: And yf I maye fynde suche a knyghte that hath all these vertues / he may drawe oute this swerd oute of the shethe / for I haue ben at kyng Ryons / it was told me ther were passyng good knyghtes / and he and alle his knyghtes haue assayed it and none can spede(please add an English translation of this quotation)

quote.citation: c. 1596–1598 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Merchant of Venice”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene i]:
quote.text: We have been praying for our husbands' healths,Which speed, we hope, the better for our words.Are they returned?

quote.text: At night returning, every labor sped, / He sits him down the monarch of a shed: / Smiles by his cheerful fire, and round surveys, / His children’s looks, that brighten at the blaze;

definitions.definition: (transitive, archaic) To help someone, to give them fortune; to aid or favour.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To go fast.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To exceed the speed limit.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To increase the rate at which something occurs.

definitions.definition: (intransitive, slang) To be under the influence of stimulant drugs, especially amphetamines.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) To be expedient.
(archaic) To hurry to destruction; to put an end to; to ruin.
